History:
• 35-year-old male presents with intermittent severe frontal headaches that “come and go” primarily while at work (during meetings or computer use).  
• Onset: Shortly after changing jobs (exact time frame not specified).  
• Associated symptoms (occur at separate times, not always together):  
  – Mild nausea with some headache episodes.  
  – Reduced appetite with unintentional 5-lb weight loss.  
  – Bilateral tingling (“quick pricking”) in both hands, no leg involvement.  
  – Daily episodes of awareness of fast heartbeat (palpitations).  
  – Occasional shortness of breath while seated at desk; none with exercise.  
  – Decreased libido, onset concurrent with job change.  
• Stress level estimated 7–8/10 since starting new job as lawyer; prior baseline similar but patient feels current symptoms are new.  
• No prior history of headaches. No radiation of pain, no noted visual changes, aura, or limb weakness.

Past Medical History:
• Hyperthyroidism (patient-reported).  
• Medications: Thyroxine (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• Allergies: Not documented.  
• Social: Alcohol—couple of glasses of wine once weekly.  Non-smoker.  Denies recreational drug use.

Physical Examination:
• Remote video visit; no formal examination performed.  
• Patient appears alert, oriented, speaking in full sentences. No acute distress observed.

Impression:
• New-onset headaches with systemic symptoms (palpitations, weight loss, paresthesias); differential includes thyroid dysfunction, stress/anxiety-related disorder, or other metabolic/neurologic etiology.

Management Plan:
• Arrange in-person clinic appointment for full physical examination (cardiac, respiratory, neurologic).  
• Order blood tests including thyroid function panel.  
• No new medications started; continue current thyroxine until review.  
• Document consultation summary for next clinician.  
• Patient to self-book through the clinic app; advised to attend promptly.

Patient Summary:
Mr. Smith, 35, developed work-associated frontal headaches plus palpitations, hand tingling, mild weight loss, and low libido since starting a new, high-stress legal job. Given his history of thyroid disease and current symptoms, he requires face-to-face assessment and thyroid labs to rule out metabolic causes and assess stress-related contributions.

Key Takeaways:
• Book an in-person visit as soon as possible.  
• Expect blood tests (thyroid panel) at that visit; continue current medication until results known.  
• Return earlier if headaches worsen suddenly, vision changes, or severe shortness of breath develop.

Next Steps:
• Clinic to perform full physical exam and vital signs.  
• Order comprehensive thyroid profile; add CBC, electrolytes as indicated.  
• Reassess medication dose after lab results.  
• Consider stress management strategies after organic causes addressed.
